title: The Sentence at the Table: dominus Orlando de Cataniis and the Gift of La Verna
years: fl. 1213-1236; died between 6 May 1236 and 4 September 1237
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the fief granted in 967
stops.date_confidence: attested for the grant, unproven for the descent: it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna' records the 967 investiture of Goffredo del fu Ildebrando di Catenaia by Otto I. The gathered brief added a day, 7 December, and a place of issue, Ostia; neither is attested anywhere reachable, and Ostia does not sit on Otto I's autumn itinerary, which ran Verona, Ravenna, Rome for the coronation of 25 December. Both dropped. Whether the later Catani of Chiusi descend from this Goffredo cannot be demonstrated.
stops.campa: An imperial act of Otto I invests Goffredo, son of the late Ildebrando di Catenaia, with the castle and the country under the mountain: Verghereto, Pieve Santo Stefano, Badia Tedalda, Sarna, Compito, Vezzano, Chitignano. One parchment fixes a name to a rock at the head of the Casentino and hands it a valley's worth of dependent villages. Whether the man who will give La Verna away descends from this Goffredo is not demonstrable; the two ends of the chain are held apart by two and a half centuries of missing links. The shape of the holding is what carries forward: a castle on the spur, and the villages of two valleys owing to it.
stops.quote: Goffredo del fu Ildebrando di Catenaia
stops.quote_source: it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna', naming the recipient of the 967 investiture by Otto I
suggested_refs: The 967 diploma of Otto I for Goffredo del fu Ildebrando di Catenaia
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'
en.wikipedia, 'Otto II, Holy Roman Emperor' (the 967 itinerary)

stops.name: Alpe di Catenaia, the name before the castle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the toponymic derivation is standard and it.wikipedia styles both the 967 recipient and the 1261 brothers di Catenaia, but no source dates the family's move from the massif to Chiusi. The year here only orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to the massif itself, summit Il Castello, 1414 m; the gathered brief had drifted about eleven kilometres north.
stops.campa: The massif rises south of the castle, a long whaleback of beech and pasture topped by the summit they call Il Castello, fourteen hundred metres above the Arno. From it the family takes the name the Aretine notaries write: di Catenaia. The Franciscan books, coming later and from elsewhere, write Cattani instead, and the codex of La Verna writes Cataniis with a double letter. The three spellings run down the centuries side by side and no document reconciles them. Nobody has dated the move from the massif to the castle either; the family is simply found at Chiusi, carrying the name of the ridge behind it.
suggested_refs: The Alpe di Catenaia, between the Arno and the Tiber headwaters
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Alpe di Catenaia'
it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: Arezzo, the bishop's captains
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, attributed to Pierluigi Licciardello and not independently verified: the study could not be retrieved this pass, and it.wikipedia's full-text search returns nothing for it. No act of Orlando's personal homage to the bishop survives; the feudal tie is inferred from the family's documented class, not from any record of him in the city. The date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: Catani is not a family name to begin with. It is capitanei, the medieval Latin for the major vassals a bishop keeps under arms, and it belongs to a class before it belongs to any household. The lords of Chiusi hold their castle and their rights of the bishop of Arezzo, inside the wider Rolandi and Ildebrandi kinship that fills the Aretine countryside with fortified spurs and disputed tithes. Across the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the office hardens into a surname. No act of Orlando's own homage to the bishop survives; the tie is inferred from the class he belongs to, not from any record of him in the city.
suggested_refs: The episcopal city of Arezzo and its capitanei of the contado
sources: Pierluigi Licciardello, reconstruction of the medieval lords of Chiusi della Verna (cited at second hand; not retrieved)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, a birth with no year
stops.date_confidence: unattested: no source gives a birth date, year, birthplace, parentage or education. 1180 is a placeholder for a man already adult and already styled dominus by the 1230s, and it carries no evidential weight.
stops.campa: No register, no chronicle, no notarial hand records the year he is born, or to whom, or where. He enters the record already grown and already styled dominus. Where a biography would want a father the sources supply none; where it would want a schooling they supply none of that either. What can be stated is the ground: a castle on the southern spur, a town beneath it, a beech mountain a mile north, and a bishop at Arezzo who considers the whole of it held from him. Whether Orlando is thirty in 1213 or fifty-five, nothing consulted allows a guess.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (sought, no retrievable entry for Orlando di Chiusi)
sources: Absence noted across Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924)
it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: Pietramala, the wife the genealogists supply
stops.date_confidence: unconfirmed tradition, and disclaimed by the man who reported it: Zeffirino Lazzeri published the Maria di Pietramala identification in 1913 and explicitly declined to affirm its truth. Lazzeri's study could not be retrieved this pass. The date is a placeholder for a marriage nobody dates. Coordinates corrected to the Tarlati seat east of Arezzo, toward Anghiari; the gathered brief had placed it west of the city, and it is not the Pietramala near Firenzuola.
stops.campa: An old genealogy gives him a wife: Maria di Pietramala, of the Tarlati, the Aretine house whose seat lies out toward Anghiari. Zeffirino Lazzeri put the identification into print in 1913, six hundred and seventy-six years after the sons she is said to have borne, and declined to say it was true. It is the only domestic fact anybody has ever offered about the man, and its author would not stand behind it. No marriage contract, no dowry instrument, no witness list carries her name.
suggested_refs: Zeffirino Lazzeri, 1913, reporting without endorsing the Maria di Pietramala tradition
sources: Zeffirino Lazzeri, 1913 (not retrieved; known only as characterised in the research brief)
it.wikipedia, 'Tarlati'

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the wolf ground while it is still his
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the mountain's tenure with the fief of Chiusi is attested, and the terrain is fixed geography, but no source dates Orlando's own use of it or places him on it. Canonical pin inherited from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: A mile north of the castle the ground climbs into cliff and beech forest, cut by ravines, roofed in one place by an overhanging rock with water running under it. Wolves work the slopes and falcons nest on the crags. It is a great deal of country worth very little: too steep to plough, too high to settle, useful to a lord as timber and hunting and as the part of a fief nobody argues about. Orlando holds it the way any lord holds his least productive corner, which is to say he holds it and leaves it alone. There is nothing on the shelf below the summit but beech, rock, and running water.
suggested_refs: The forest, cliffs, spring and Sasso Spicco of Monte della Verna, upper Casentino
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'
it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: San Leo, the crag and the knighting
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the tradition is contradicted by its own source: the earliest narrative, the Prima Considerazione of the Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, names the setting only Castello di Montefeltro and dates the episode to 1224. San Leo is a later gloss, defensible because San Leo was the seat of the Montefeltro. The pin is inherited byte-identical from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: The capital of the Montefeltro stands on a single rock with vertical sides and one cut road up. A count of the country is being made a knight, and the lords ride in for the feast, Orlando among them, out of Tuscany and over the watershed into Romagna. The friar from Assisi is in the district and the company sends for him. The civic record of San Leo, when it speaks of the year at all, says only that Francis passed through. Everything else that happens inside that hall reaches later ages through devotional books, written a century afterward by men who were not in the room.
stops.quote: uno grande convito, e corteo per la cavalleria nuova d'uno di quelli Conti di Montefeltro
stops.quote_source: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource), on the occasion of the feast
suggested_refs: The rocca of San Leo, historic capital of the Montefeltro
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)
saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'San Leo, the verse of the castle feast and the gift of La Verna'

stops.name: San Leo, the friar on the wall
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sermon on the courtyard wall is narrated only in the fourteenth-century Considerazioni, more than a century after the alleged event. No contemporary document mentions the preaching, the audience, or Orlando's presence.
stops.campa: Francis climbs onto a low wall in the courtyard and preaches on two lines of vernacular verse, a couplet in the meter of love songs turned to another use. The subject is pain taken as joy. He is speaking the language these knights hear sung at every other table in the Romagna, to men who have ridden up in mail for a knighting. Orlando stands in the crowd as a neighbour and a guest, in from Tuscany for a knighting, listening to a beggar on a wall talk about pain. When the preaching stops he does not go back to his seat.
suggested_refs: The courtyard of the rocca of San Leo, setting of the sermon in the Prima Considerazione
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)

stops.name: San Leo, the counsel asked and deferred
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the exchange survives only in the Considerazioni. It is the sole report of anything Orlando said or thought, and it is a devotional formula recorded a hundred years later.
stops.campa: When the sermon ends the count comes to Francis and asks for counsel about the salvation of his soul. It is a formula, and it is also the entire surviving contents of his interior life: one sentence, asked standing at a party by a lord in his prime, of a beggar, in front of an armed hall. Francis will not take a man out of his obligations, not even toward himself. Go and pay respect to your friends, he answers, who have bidden you to this feast, and dine with them; afterwards we will talk as long as you like. The count goes back and eats.
suggested_refs: The great hall of the rocca of San Leo
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)

stops.name: San Leo, the mountain offered after dinner
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the quotation needs its own caution: the gathered brief supplied a composite text carrying the phrases e salvatico and in luogo rimosso dalle gente, which the Wikisource text of the Prima Considerazione does not have. The quote here is the Wikisource wording, elided at the ellipsis. No charter, notarial instrument or contemporary record of the donation survives at all.
stops.campa: After dinner he makes the offer. He has a mountain in Tuscany, most devout and most solitary, well fitted to a man who wants to do penance far from people, and he will give it away for the good of his soul. He asks no rent, no service, no reservation of the timber or the hunting; the consideration named is the welfare of his own soul, and the beneficiary is a man who owns nothing and has taken a vow against owning. The whole conveyance is one sentence spoken at a table in another lord's castle, between two courses. No charter is drawn and no notary is called.
stops.quote: Io ho in Toscana uno Monte divotissimo, il quale si chiama il Monte della Vernia, il quale è molto solitario, ed è troppo bene atto a chi volesse fare penitenza... s'egli ti piacesse, volentieri lo ti donerei a te, e a' tuoi compagni
stops.quote_source: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource, 'Delle sacre sante stimmate di San Francesco')
suggested_refs: The Prima Considerazione, sole narrative source for the donation of La Verna
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)

stops.name: San Leo, the year the oldest text actually gives
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, NOT resolved: devotional tradition and the sanctuary's painted memory give 8 May 1213; the Prima Considerazione, the oldest narrative of the scene, opens by dating it to 1224 with Francis aged forty-three. The gathered brief said the earliest narrative gives no exact date, only 'in that year'. That is false, and the correction makes the traditional date harder to hold, not easier. Both years are carried; neither is adjudicated here.
stops.campa: The books do not agree about when this happens. Devotional tradition and the sanctuary's own painted memory fix it at 8 May 1213. The oldest surviving narrative of the scene fixes it somewhere else entirely: Francis aged forty-three, in the year twelve hundred twenty-four, the year of the stigmata itself. The text that supplies every vivid detail of the feast contradicts the date those details are always hung on. Nothing survives from either year to settle it, and the two stand eleven years apart inside one tradition.
stops.quote: san Francesco essendo in età di quarantatrè anni, nel mille dugento ventiquattro, ispirato da Dio, si mosse della Valle di Spuleto
stops.quote_source: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione, opening lines (it.wikisource)
suggested_refs: it.wikisource, 'Delle sacre sante stimmate di San Francesco'
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the count rides home
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the return follows the feast in the narrative sequence of the Prima Considerazione, which gives the distance between castle and mountain as about a mile. No source dates the ride.
stops.campa: He rides back over the passes to his own rock. The distance matters and the narrative is careful with it: about a mile between the castle and the mountain. What he has given away stands in sight of his windows. From the spur where the tower sits a man can look up the slope at property that is no longer his, and nobody has yet walked on it under the new arrangement. Nothing at Chiusi is told to change. The beech wood on the height looks in June exactly as it looked in April.
suggested_refs: The Cassero of Chiusi della Verna, on the southern spur above the town
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)
it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the escort against the wolves
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the reception of the two friars and the escort of fifty armed men are narrated only in the Prima Considerazione. No charter, chronicle or account book corroborates them, and none of the fifty is named.
stops.campa: Two friars come to the castle as promised, and the count does the one thing a lord can do that a mendicant cannot. He feeds them, lodges them, and then puts fifty armed men at their backs for the climb, against the wolves. The ground they are to inspect begins a mile north of his gate. It is the only act of his that any account describes in operational detail: a fighting household emptied out for two men in habits walking up a hill within sight of the walls. Not one of the fifty is named.
suggested_refs: The castle hall of Chiusi, where the Prima Considerazione places the reception of the two friars
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the friars find it fit
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the inspection belongs entirely to the Prima Considerazione, and no source places Orlando himself on the climb. Canonical pin inherited from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: They come out on the shelf under the crags and find what he described at the table: forest, cliff, water, a place remote from the discourse of men. They are the first men sent up the mountain on Francis's account, and they climb it as surveyors rather than as hermits. The report goes back down the valley and the provisional gift becomes a real one. Two men were sent to look at a wood and have come back saying the wood will do. Nothing in the narrative says how long they stayed on the height, or where they slept, or whether the fifty waited.
suggested_refs: The spring on the sanctuary shelf of La Verna
sources: Fioretti di san Francesco, Considerazioni sulle sacre sante stimmate, Prima Considerazione (it.wikisource)
it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'

stops.name: La Verna, the first cell under the Sasso Spicco
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' places the first cell of wood and earth near the Sasso Spicco, but fixes no year, and no source puts Orlando there at any time. The date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: Below the shelf the rock overhangs in a great cleft, a roofed emptiness of stone with water running somewhere under it. Near this the first cell is raised, of wood and earth. No source puts the count under this rock at any hour of his life, and nobody has drawn a boundary inside the donation: the mountain went whole, cliffs, spring, cleft, timber, wolves and all. Orlando's title to every part of it ended with one spoken sentence at another lord's feast. What stands on the mountain now is a hut of wood and earth under an overhanging rock.
suggested_refs: The Sasso Spicco, below the sanctuary of La Verna
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'

stops.name: La Verna, the chapel of Santa Maria degli Angeli begun
stops.date_confidence: attested for the building, unsupported for the financing: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' dates construction of the first chapel to 1216-1218, begun at Francis's request. The claim that Orlando helped pay for it appears only in weakly sourced devotional accounts; no reachable account of the chapel names any lay financier, and later compilers do not say which Orlando they mean.
stops.campa: The friars begin a church on the shelf at Francis's own asking, and the sanctuary's memory holds that the Virgin of the Angels showed him the site and the measurements in a dream, so that the walls go up to dimensions received asleep. Devotional accounts add that Orlando helps to pay for it. No account book, no legacy, no receipt supports the addition, and the compilers who repeat it do not trouble to say which Orlando they mean. Building runs from 1216.
suggested_refs: The Cappella di Santa Maria degli Angeli, La Verna, first permanent building on the mountain
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'

segments.name: The Wounds on the Given Ground

stops.name: La Verna, the chapel standing
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' gives construction 1216-1218, enlargement from about 1250 under Cardinal Rainaldo da Segni, consecration of the enlarged church in 1260 with Bonaventure present. Orlando was dead more than twenty years before that consecration.
stops.campa: By 1218 the little church stands, the first work in stone on a height that had carried nothing but a cell of wood and earth. Five years earlier there were wolves on it and a spring and no roof of any kind. From the walls of Chiusi the new masonry shows as a pale mark under the summit. Thirty-odd years later the friars enlarge it, and in 1260 the enlarged church is consecrated with Bonaventure present, the shell of the first chapel standing inside the bigger building. Orlando has been dead more than twenty years by then.
suggested_refs: The enlarged nave of Santa Maria degli Angeli, consecrated 1260
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the years without a document
stops.date_confidence: gap: no source places Orlando anywhere, or records any act of his, between the donation narrative and the notarial instrument of 6 May 1236. The date is a placeholder inside that silence.
stops.campa: For the length of a generation the man is missing from his own story. No second meeting with Francis is recorded, no ride up to the shelf, no letter, no lawsuit, no witness list, no oath. The Franciscan writers have no further use for him once the mountain is theirs, and the Aretine notaries have not yet had cause to write his name down. He goes on doing what a lord of Chiusi does: holding a castle, judging his men, taking what the fief renders, answering to a bishop at Arezzo.
sources: Absence noted across Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (1924)
it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the seraph on land he gave away
stops.date_confidence: attested in Franciscan tradition, and not this file's event: the stigmata is Francis's own, recorded on saint_francis.journey.json with its own apparatus, the Chartula of Assisi among it. It stands here once, as the consequence of the donation, and is not restaged. Canonical pin inherited from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: Francis keeps a forty-day fast on the mountain with Brother Leo and three companions, and takes on his body the five wounds. It happens on land a Casentine lord gave away without a notary and without witnesses, for the welfare of his soul. This is the event that makes the gift matter, and it is not Orlando's event. The seraph, the rock, the fast and the wounds belong to Francis of Assisi, whose own record carries them. Orlando is a mile downhill at his castle, and no source says he is told, that week or ever.
suggested_refs: The Cappella delle Stimmate, La Verna, built over the place of the wounds
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'La Verna, the seraph and the stigmata'
it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, whether word came down the mile
stops.date_confidence: gap: no source records that Orlando learned of the stigmata, when he learned, or what he said. Nothing here is asserted beyond the silence, and the date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: A mile below the shelf stands a castle. Nothing in any source says word came down to it, or that the count went up, or that anyone thought to tell him. He is the nearest lord and the donor of the ground, and the record does not give him a sentence. The silence is not evidence that he was indifferent and it is not evidence that he was moved. Did anyone at Chiusi hear of it that autumn? The books that tell the story of the wounds do not think to say.
sources: Gap noted across it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna', it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna', and Mencherini's Codice diplomatico

stops.name: Poppi, the Guidi castle and the seller
stops.date_confidence: attested for the transaction, unresolved for the man: Mencherini's regesto names the seller Guidone de Puppio, Guido of Poppi. Which Guido this is could not be established, since the Guidi succession at Poppi in the 1230s is not documented in anything reachable. Coordinates corrected to the town; the gathered brief lay about a kilometre and a half south of it.
stops.campa: The Guidi hold the valley from a castle on a knoll above the Arno, the strongest house in the Casentino and no kin at all to the captains of Chiusi. Which Guido of Poppi sells in the spring of 1236 cannot be established; the succession there in that decade is not documented in anything reachable. The parchment gives a name, Guidone de Puppio, and a transaction: a podere in the territory of Chiusi, with its houses and its yards, sold to the lord of the castle under the mountain.
suggested_refs: The Castello dei Conti Guidi at Poppi, above the Casentino
sources: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924), p. 685
it.wikipedia, 'Poppi'

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the instrument of 6 May 1236
stops.date_confidence: attested, and verified directly in the primary edition the gathering pass could not open: Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924), p. 685, regesto of the instrument. The brief supplied a nominative form, nobilis vir Orlandus de Catanis de castro Clusii, which appears nowhere in the edition; a full-text search for nobilis vir returns one hit, on p. 181, in an unrelated letter salutation. The correct wording is the genitive governed by ad favorem, quoted here.
stops.campa: On the sixth of May a notary draws the instrument, and for the first time in his life the man is written down in a way that survives. The Latin styles him spectabilis ac nobilis vir, and nothing else. He is buying, not giving: a podere in the territory of the castle of Chiusi, with its buildings and its open ground. Twenty-three years after the sentence at the table, if the traditional date is the right one, the donor of La Verna is in a notary's hands buying a farm.
stops.quote: ad favorem spectabilis ac nobilis viri Orlandi de Cataniis de Castro Clusii, cum casamentis, plateis
stops.quote_source: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924), p. 685, regesto of the instrument of 6 May 1236
suggested_refs: Mencherini's Codice diplomatico della Verna, archive.org item codicediplomatic0000disf
sources: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924), p. 685

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the title no notary wrote
stops.date_confidence: attested by absence, and checked against the primary edition: the phrase de castro Clusii occurs four times in the whole codex, pp. 123, 199, 685, 690, and on three of those it is a place-of-action formula rather than a style of the lords. Comes de Clusio appears at p. 64 and de Clusi at pp. 62 and 66, for other men and other centuries. The date only holds this stop beside the instrument it comments on.
stops.campa: He is never called count in his own century. The documents give him dominus, which is messere, the ordinary style of any lord of a castle; they give him nobilis vir and spectabilis vir; they place him de Cataniis and de Castro Clusii. Comes turns up elsewhere in the codex, for other men of Chiusi in other decades, but not in the act that is his. The count is a later promotion, granted by writers who found dominus too small for the man who gave a mountain to a saint. No parchment of his own century supports it.
stops.quote: Nobilis vir ac maior bonus, pax tibi et salus a Deo
stops.quote_source: Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate, p. 181: the codex's only occurrence of the phrase nobilis vir, in an unrelated letter salutation and not in any act naming Orlando
suggested_refs: The styles dominus, nobilis vir and spectabilis vir in the Codice diplomatico della Verna
sources: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924), pp. 62, 64, 66, 123, 181, 199, 685, 690

stops.name: Abbey of Santa Fiora, quondam domini Orlandi
stops.date_confidence: attested: Mencherini's codex records dominus Orlandus quondam domini Orlandi lending money to the abbey. The act is the son's; it is entered here because the two words quondam domini are the only record of the father's death that exists.
stops.campa: Sixteen months after the purchase a lender comes to the abbey with money for the monks, and is written into the act as dominus Orlandus quondam domini Orlandi. Orlando, son of the late lord Orlando. The son now holds the name and the styles, and two words in a routine loan are the only notice of the father's death that anyone kept. On the fourth of September 1237 the man who spoke at the table in the Montefeltro is already dead. The act does not say when.
stops.quote_source: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate, document of 4 September 1237 (as relayed in the research brief; the folio itself was not opened)
suggested_refs: The abbey of Santa Fiora in the Aretine territory
sources: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924)
Pierluigi Licciardello, reconstruction of the medieval lords of Chiusi della Verna (cited at second hand; not retrieved)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, a death sixteen months wide
stops.date_confidence: attested only as an interval: after 6 May 1236 and before 4 September 1237. No cause, no exact day, no place of death and no burial record survives. Family burial at Santa Maria degli Angeli is documented for later descendants of the line, not for the donor himself.
stops.campa: His death is a gap sixteen months wide, bounded at one end by a land purchase and at the other by a preposition in his son's contract. No deathbed, no illness, no will, no anniversary, no grave. Later descendants of the house are buried at Santa Maria degli Angeli on the mountain; for the donor himself there is no interment record anywhere, at La Verna or at Chiusi or in the Aretine countryside. No document has ever been produced for a specific tomb.
sources: Saturnino Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, nothing in his own hand
stops.date_confidence: attested by absence across Mencherini's codex: every surviving document naming Orlando is a legal or notarial record of a transaction involving him, never a text he composed. The date is a placeholder just past the death window.
stops.campa: No book, no treatise, no poem, no letter of his is known, and nobody claims one ever existed. Every surviving document that names him is a legal record of something happening to his property: a sale, a boundary, a favour, a loan made by his heir. He is a man assembled entirely out of other people's paperwork and one remembered sentence, and the sentence itself survives only because a friar in the Marches wrote it down a century after it was spoken. There is no hand of his.
sources: Absence noted across Mencherini, Codice diplomatico della Verna e delle SS. Stimate (Florence, 1924)

stops.name: Sarna, the podesteria of 1250
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a correction: popular accounts give the office to the donor, who had been dead thirteen years. The 1250 podesteria itself could not be verified in anything reachable. Coordinates corrected to the frazione of Chiusi della Verna; the gathered brief placed Sarna on the valley floor outside the comune. It.wikipedia does list Sarna among the villages of the 967 fief, so the family's tie to the place is real.
stops.campa: Sarna lies among the villages the act of 967 named, a hamlet of the same fief on the flank of the ridge. In 1250 an Orlando holds the podesteria there, and popular accounts hand the office to the count who gave La Verna away. He cannot have held it. He has been dead thirteen years. The Orlando of Sarna is his son, who carries the name and the styles and, in the accounts that merge the two men, most of the father's afterlife as well. The podesteria itself could not be confirmed in anything reachable.

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the bishop takes the country back
stops.date_confidence: attested for the act, and explicitly not the donor's: it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna' names the three brothers Orlando, Alberto and Niccolo di Catenaia left with the castle alone. This Orlando is the son. The donor had been dead twenty-four years, and local histories that fold this quarrel into his life are the reason his biography appears to run a hundred years.
stops.campa: Guglielmino degli Ubertini, bishop of Arezzo, asserts his own lordship over the country the family has held since the tenth century, and leaves the brothers Orlando, Alberto and Niccolo di Catenaia the castle of Chiusi and nothing else. The house keeps its rock and loses the valley. The mountain the donor gave away is by then in the hands of friars and is no part of what the bishop claims. The Orlando in this act is the son, in a quarrel his father never lived to have. The father had been dead twenty-four years.

stops.name: Arezzo, the letters nobody can produce
stops.date_confidence: unattested, and the exclusion is stronger than the brief made it: Guittone d'Arezzo was born between 1230 and 1240 per the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, so he was at most seven when the donor died. The DBI also lists Guittone's known correspondents and dedicatees, Marzucco Iscornigiano, Guido Guidi, Loderengo Andalo among them, and includes no Orlando of Chiusi at all, noting only that the recipients of some letters remain obscure.
stops.campa: A correspondence between Guittone d'Arezzo and an Orlando of Chiusi is sometimes mentioned. The poet was born between 1230 and 1240, which puts him at most seven years old when the donor of La Verna died, so the letters, if they exist, cannot be to him. They may not exist at all. The standard biographical account lists Guittone's correspondents and dedicatees by name, Marzucco Iscornigiano, Guido Guidi, Loderengo Andalo, and there is no Orlando among them. It says only that the recipients of some letters remain obscure.

stops.name: Campaldino, the counsel in nobody's chronicle
stops.date_confidence: date and place attested, the episode not: en. and it.wikipedia fix the battle to 11 June 1289 on the plain between Poppi and Pratovecchio, near the church of Certomondo. Neither account mentions any Orlando di Chiusi advising the Florentines; the named commanders and advisers are Amerigo di Narbona, Guillaume de Durfort, Corso Donati, Vieri de' Cerchi, Barone dei Mangiadori, Bindo degli Adimari, Ugolino de' Rossi. This is popular tradition with no traceable source, not a real episode misfiled. Coordinates corrected by about 2.4 km from the gathered brief.
stops.campa: On the plain between Poppi and Pratovecchio, near the little church of Certomondo on the left bank of the Arno, the Florentine army breaks the Aretine host. Guglielmino degli Ubertini, the bishop who stripped the family of its valley twenty-eight years earlier, is killed in the field. Tradition puts an Orlando di Chiusi at the Florentine councils beforehand, giving advice. No account of the battle names him, on either side, among the commanders or the counsellors. The donor of La Verna has been dead fifty-two years.

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the confirmation of 1274
stops.date_confidence: reported, not tested: the forgery verdict on the 1274 confirmation comes from modern diplomatic analysis as relayed through Licciardello's reconstruction, which could not be retrieved this pass. The instrument itself was not opened, reproduced or seen. The month and day are unknown.
stops.campa: Sixty-one years after the traditional date of the gift, an instrument appears confirming the terms of the donation of La Verna. Modern diplomatic analysis calls it a forgery, but a forgery of a particular kind: assembled out of genuine family documents rather than invented from nothing, made because the friars now need a parchment where a lord once needed only his word. For centuries the details of the gift were fixed from it. No original has ever been produced, before 1274 or since.

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the century-late book that supplies everything
stops.date_confidence: attested for the text, interpretive for its placement: the Actus beati Francisci et sociorum eius is attributed to Ugolino Brunforte da Montegiorgio and dated by it.wikipedia between 1322 and 1337 depending on the page, so it is given here as c.1320s-1340s. The stop sits at Orlando's own castle, not at Montegiorgio in the Marche, which is Ugolino's place and one Orlando never went near. The year only orders the segment.
stops.campa: A friar of the Marches sets down the story of the feast and the mountain: the sermon, the sentence at the table, the fifty men-at-arms, the wood found fit. He is writing something between 1320 and 1345, a hundred years and more after the events. Everything vivid about Orlando comes from these pages and from nowhere earlier; outside them he is a land purchase, a loan made by his son, and a name in a notary's Latin. The vernacular adaptation of the book will carry the scene into every Italian household as the Fioretti.

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the arms the town paints for him
stops.date_confidence: later civic memory, not personal arms: it.wikipedia gives the comune's blazon as di rosso, alla fascia cucita di azzurro, caricata di tre gigli d'oro, sormontata da una croce gigliata dello stesso, which is a cross flory, not a plain gilded cross as the gathered brief rendered it. No seal or shield of Orlando's own survives on any act. The date is a placeholder and carries no evidential weight.
stops.campa: The comune carries arms: gules, a fess azure charged with three fleurs-de-lis or, surmounted by a cross flory of the same. They are painted on the walls of a town that remembers a count, and they are civic memory rather than evidence. No seal of Orlando's survives, no shield, no impression in wax on any of the acts that name him. A house of episcopal captains in the thirteenth century may well have borne something. Whether it bore this cannot be shown.

stops.name: La Verna, two canvases of 1877
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' records two canvases of 1877 by the Florentine painter Ferdinando Folchi on the walls before the tramezzo of Santa Maria degli Angeli, one showing the meeting of Francis and Orlando at San Leo.
stops.campa: The Florentine painter Ferdinando Folchi delivers two canvases for the chapel of Santa Maria degli Angeli, hung on the walls before the tramezzo. One shows Francis meeting Count Orlando Catani at the fortress of San Leo. No source records what the man looked like, so the face is Folchi's, and the title lettered over the face is the one no notary ever wrote. The scene is dated 1213 by the sanctuary and 1224 by the oldest text that tells it. The canvases have hung in the chapel since 1877.
